content.intro: This lesson focuses on json and yaml professional best practices and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: JSON and YAML Professional Best Practices matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Advanced workflows combine data modeling, schema composition, parser portability, transformation pipelines, streaming, canonicalization, and operational documentation. Use specialized features only when their compatibility and security implications are understood.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: Prefer simple, predictable data structures. Use consistent field names. Keep data types explicit where ambiguity is possible.; Validate untrusted and externally supplied data. Use compatible standards and parser settings. Document schema versions.; Avoid unsupported tags and parser-specific extensions when portability matters.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: JSON and YAML Professional Best Practices
content_blocks.code:
Professional baseline:
- Explicit schema and parser versions
- Valid, invalid, and boundary tests
- No secrets in the repository or logs
- Stable names and documented null/date rules
- Reviewed semantic diffs and migrations
- Clear owners and rollback guidance
content_blocks.expected_output: Structured-data quality is an ongoing engineering practice that combines readable files with contracts, security, testing, and maintenance.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Advanced features are useful only when all relevant tools agree on their semantics. Prefer the simplest portable representation that meets the requirement. Confirm implementation-specific behavior against the target parser, tool version, and standards documentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
